proof_text:
Suppose for contradiction that there exists a bijection
$f : A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$. In particular, $f$ must be surjective.
Define the diagonal subset $D \subseteq A$ by Separation:
$$D := \{x \in A : x \notin f(x)\}$$ Because $D \subseteq A$, $D$ is
an element of the power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$. Since $f$ is surjective
onto $\mathcal{P}(A)$, there must exist an element $d \in A$ such that
$f(d) = D$. Now ask whether $d \in D$:
- If $d \in D$, then by definition of $D$, $d \notin f(d) = D$, which
  is an immediate contradiction.
- If $d \notin D$, then $d \notin f(d)$, which by definition of $D$
  implies $d \in D$, again a contradiction. Thus
  $d \in D \iff d \notin D$, which is a logical impossibility.
  Therefore no surjective function from $A$ to $\mathcal{P}(A)$ can
  exist, proving that $A$ is not equinumerous with $\mathcal{P}(A)$.
